q: SI unit of absorbed dose?
explain: Absorbed dose is energy per unit mass: 1 Gy = 1 J/kg. Sievert is for equivalent/effective dose.

q: 1 Gy equals how many rad?
explain: 1 Gy = 100 rad.

q: Radiation weighting factor (wR) for diagnostic X-rays is:
explain: X-rays, gamma and beta have wR = 1; alpha particles have wR = 20.

q: Unit of radioactivity in SI?
explain: 1 Bq = 1 disintegration per second.

q: Characteristic X-rays are produced when:
options: An electron decelerates near the nucleus
An outer-shell electron fills an inner-shell vacancy
A photon is scattered by a free electron
A nucleus emits a gamma ray
explain: The energy difference between the two shells is emitted as a characteristic photon.

q: Bremsstrahlung radiation results from:
options: Deceleration of electrons near the nucleus
explain: It gives a continuous spectrum, maximum photon energy equals the kVp.

q: Approximate minimum kVp needed to produce tungsten K-characteristic X-rays?
explain: The K-shell binding energy of tungsten is about 69.5 keV.

q: The anode heel effect causes the beam intensity to be:
explain: X-rays travel a longer path inside the target toward the anode side, so intensity is lower there.

q: Which target material is commonly used in mammography?
explain: Mo (and Rh) give characteristic X-rays of about 17-20 keV, suited for breast tissue contrast.

q: Probability of photoelectric effect is approximately proportional to:
explain: Photoelectric absorption varies as Z^3/E^3, which is why contrast media with high Z work.

q: Main source of scatter radiation fogging in diagnostic radiography:
explain: Compton scatter dominates in soft tissue at higher diagnostic energies.

q: Threshold energy for pair production is:
explain: Two electron rest masses: 2 x 511 keV = 1.022 MeV.

q: Half-value layer (HVL) is the thickness of material that:
explain: After 3 HVLs the intensity falls to 1/8 (12.5%).

q: If distance from a point source is doubled, intensity becomes:
explain: Inverse square law: I is proportional to 1/d^2.

q: ICRP occupational effective dose limit (averaged over 5 years)?
explain: 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years, with no single year above 50 mSv.

q: Three basic principles of protection against external radiation:
explain: Minimise time, maximise distance, use shielding.

q: Physical half-life of Tc-99m is about:
explain: About 6 hours, emitting 140 keV gamma rays.

q: Gamma photon energy of Tc-99m?
explain: 140 keV, ideal for gamma cameras.

q: Mo-99/Tc-99m generator operates in:
explain: Parent half-life (66 h) is only moderately longer than daughter's (6 h): transient equilibrium.

q: Positron annihilation produces:
options: Two 511 keV photons at about 180 degrees
explain: This is the basis of PET coincidence detection.

q: After 3 half-lives, the fraction of radioactivity remaining is:
Larmor frequency of hydrogen at 1.5 T is approximately:
explain: 42.58 MHz/T x 1.5 T = about 63.9 MHz.

q: T1 relaxation refers to:
explain: T1 is spin-lattice relaxation; T2 is decay of transverse magnetisation.

q: Average speed of sound in soft tissue assumed by scanners:
explain: 1540 m/s is used for depth calculation.

q: Greatest reflection occurs at which interface?
explain: Large acoustic impedance mismatch causes strong reflection, hence the need for coupling gel.

q: Doppler shift is zero when the beam-flow angle is:
explain: Shift is proportional to cos(theta); cos 90 = 0.

q: Hounsfield unit of water and air respectively:
explain: Water = 0 HU, air = -1000 HU.

q: Fat typically measures approximately:
explain: Fat is about -120 to -90 HU.

q: Grid ratio is defined as:
explain: Higher ratio cleans more scatter but needs more exposure.

q: Unit used to express spatial resolution:
explain: Higher lp/mm means better spatial resolution.

q: The number of protons in the nucleus determines the chemical identity of an atom.
explain: The atomic number Z (number of protons) defines the element.

q: Isotopes of an element have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons.
explain: Isotopes have the same Z (protons) but different N (neutrons).

q: Alpha particles are more penetrating than gamma rays.
explain: Alpha particles are heavy and charged and are stopped by paper or skin. Gamma rays penetrate far more.

q: X-rays are deflected by magnetic fields.
explain: X-rays are uncharged photons, so magnetic fields do not deflect them.

q: Ultrasound is a mechanical wave and cannot travel through a vacuum.
explain: Sound needs a medium to propagate; electromagnetic waves do not.

q: The source of electrons in an X-ray tube is the:
explain: Electrons are released from the heated filament (cathode) by thermionic emission.

q: The filament of a diagnostic X-ray tube is made of:
explain: Thoriated tungsten gives efficient thermionic emission and has a very high melting point.

q: Tungsten is used as the target material in general radiography mainly because of its:
options: Low atomic number and low cost
High atomic number and high melting point
explain: Efficiency of X-ray production rises with Z, and a high melting point tolerates intense heating.

q: Approximate melting point of tungsten?
explain: Tungsten melts at about 3422 °C, which suits the high heat load on the anode.

q: Approximately what percentage of the electron kinetic energy is converted to heat at the anode?
explain: Only about 1% becomes X-rays; the rest (about 99%) is heat.

q: Tube current (mA) is controlled mainly by changing the:
explain: Raising filament current heats the filament more and releases more electrons, so mA rises.

q: The space charge effect is the:
options: Leakage of X-rays from the housing
Electron cloud around the filament that limits further electron emission
Loss of vacuum in the tube
explain: The negative electron cloud repels further electrons, mainly at low kVp.

q: Saturation current in an X-ray tube means that:
options: All emitted electrons reach the anode and mA no longer rises with kVp
explain: At high kVp the space charge is overcome; tube current then depends only on filament temperature.

q: Rhenium is alloyed with tungsten in the target to:
options: Increase the atomic number to above 100
explain: Tungsten-rhenium (about 10% Re) resists thermal damage and pitting.

q: The main purpose of a rotating anode is to:
options: Spread heat over a larger area and allow higher tube loading
explain: The electron beam strikes a continuously changing area, the focal track, so heat is not concentrated.

q: Typical rotation speed of a standard rotating anode is about:
explain: Standard stators run at about 3,400 rpm; high-speed stators run at about 9,000-10,000 rpm.

q: The line-focus principle states that:
options: The actual focal spot is smaller than the effective one
Heat is produced only in a line
The effective focal spot is smaller than the actual focal spot
explain: Because the target is angled, the focal spot seen from the image receptor is foreshortened.

q: Effective focal spot size is approximately equal to:
options: Actual focal spot size × sin (anode angle)
Actual focal spot size × cos (anode angle)
Actual focal spot size ÷ sin (anode angle)
Actual focal spot size + anode angle
explain: Reducing the target angle reduces the effective focal spot.

q: Typical anode (target) angles in diagnostic tubes are:
explain: Angles of about 12 degrees are common in general radiography tubes.

q: Decreasing the anode angle will:
options: Increase the effective focal spot and reduce the heel effect
Decrease the effective focal spot size but increase the heel effect
explain: A smaller angle gives sharper images but a larger anode heel effect and less field coverage.

q: The anode heel effect is greatest with:
options: Large anode angle and long SID
Small anode angle and short SID
explain: A steep target and a large field near the tube make intensity differences obvious.

q: In an AP thoracic spine exposure, to use the heel effect best the cathode should be placed over the:
options: Anywhere, as it makes no difference
explain: The cathode side has higher intensity, so it should cover the thicker, denser part.

q: Where is the beam intensity highest in the X-ray field?
explain: On the anode side the photons travel through more target material and are absorbed (the heel effect).

q: The small focal spot size in mammography (for magnification) is typically:
explain: Mammography uses 0.3 mm (contact) and 0.1 mm (magnification) focal spots.

q: Typical nominal focal spot sizes in general radiography are:
explain: The small spot gives sharper images; the large spot tolerates higher loading.

q: The K-characteristic X-rays of tungsten have energies of approximately:
explain: K-shell transitions in tungsten give photons of about 58-69 keV.

q: For an 80 kVp exposure the maximum photon energy in the beam is:
explain: The maximum photon energy in keV equals the peak tube voltage in kVp.

q: The average photon energy of a diagnostic X-ray beam is about:
options: One-third to one-half of the peak energy
explain: The spectrum is continuous, with most photons at lower energies.

q: The efficiency of X-ray production increases with:
options: Increasing atomic number of target and increasing kVp
explain: Efficiency is proportional to Z × kVp.

q: The function of the rectifier in an X-ray generator is to:
options: Convert alternating current to direct (unidirectional) current
explain: Rectifiers let current flow in one direction only, so the tube conducts only from cathode to anode.

q: Voltage ripple of single-phase full-wave rectified output is:
explain: The voltage swings from zero to the peak 120 times per second.

q: Approximate ripple of a 12-pulse three-phase generator is:
explain: Six-pulse gives about 13.5% ripple and 12-pulse about 3.5%.

q: Which generator type is most common in modern radiography and gives near-constant potential?
explain: High-frequency generators have under 1-2% ripple, are compact and give accurate exposures.

q: A step-up transformer in the X-ray circuit:
explain: The high-voltage transformer has more turns in the secondary coil than in the primary.

q: The transformer law states that:
explain: Voltage ratio equals the turns ratio; current changes inversely.

q: The filament circuit uses a:
explain: The filament needs a low voltage (about 10 V) but a high current (3-5 A).

q: Kilovoltage is selected by the:
explain: The autotransformer varies the voltage applied to the primary of the high-voltage transformer.

q: How many pulses per second does a single-phase full-wave rectified generator produce on a 60 Hz supply?
explain: Full-wave rectification gives two pulses per cycle.

q: A tube rating chart shows:
options: The maximum safe exposure combinations that will not damage the tube
explain: Charts plot kVp, mA and time limits for a given focal spot and generator type.

q: The heat unit (single-phase) is calculated as:
explain: Three-phase 6-pulse multiplies by 1.35, and 12-pulse by 1.41.

q: Heat is dissipated from the anode in a vacuum mainly by:
explain: The anode glows and radiates heat to the housing oil, where it is carried away by conduction and convection.

q: Oil is placed around the glass tube in the housing to:
explain: Oil insulates the high voltage and carries heat away.

q: Maximum permitted leakage radiation from the tube housing at 1 m is:
explain: The lead lining in the housing limits leakage radiation to this level.

q: The vacuum inside the X-ray tube is needed to:
options: Prevent electron collisions with gas molecules and filament oxidation
explain: Gas would stop electrons and oxidise the filament.

q: Off-focus radiation is produced by:
options: Electrons striking areas of the anode outside the focal spot
explain: It reduces image sharpness and increases patient dose; collimation near the tube reduces it.

q: Vaporised tungsten deposited on the inner glass envelope can cause:
explain: Over time the metal coating changes the potential inside the tube and the tube may fail.

q: A tube warm-up procedure is performed to:
options: Heat the anode gradually and avoid thermal shock
explain: Gradual heating prevents cracking of the cold anode.

q: Inherent filtration of an X-ray tube is typically equivalent to about:
explain: It comes from the glass window, the oil and the housing window.

q: Minimum total filtration for tubes operating above 70 kVp is:
explain: Regulations require at least 2.5 mm Al to remove low-energy photons.

q: The focusing cup surrounding the filament is:
options: Negatively charged and focuses electrons toward the target
explain: The negative cup repels the electrons into a narrow beam.

q: The Duane-Hunt law relates:
options: The minimum wavelength of the X-ray spectrum to the tube voltage
explain: λmin (nm) = 1.24 / kVp, which sets the maximum photon energy.

q: If mAs is doubled and everything else is constant, X-ray output (intensity) will:
explain: The number of photons is directly proportional to mAs.

q: X-ray beam intensity is approximately proportional to:
explain: Small changes in kVp change the output substantially.

q: Increasing kVp shifts the X-ray spectrum:
options: To higher energies with greater total intensity
To lower energies with less intensity
To lower energies with greater intensity
explain: The maximum and average photon energies, and the photon number, all increase.

q: Adding filtration to the beam will:
options: Decrease average energy and increase intensity
Increase average energy and decrease intensity
explain: Low-energy photons are preferentially removed, so the beam is hardened.

q: Characteristic X-rays of tungsten appear in the spectrum only when kVp is:
explain: The tube voltage must exceed the K-shell binding energy (69.5 keV).

q: Stationary anode tubes are used in:
options: Dental and some portable units where loading is low
explain: They are simple and cheap, but their heat capacity is limited.

q: The focal track of a rotating anode is:
options: The circular area of the target struck by electrons
explain: Heat is spread over this ring as the anode rotates.

q: The molybdenum stem of a rotating anode helps to:
options: Reduce heat conduction to the rotor bearings
explain: Molybdenum is a poor heat conductor and also lightweight.

q: A graphite backing on the anode disc:
options: Stores heat and increases the heat capacity
explain: Graphite has high heat capacity and low weight, so it improves heat storage.

q: Half-value layer (HVL) is the thickness of a material that:
options: Reduces beam intensity to half its original value
explain: HVL is a measure of beam quality (penetrating power).

q: A higher HVL for a given beam indicates:
explain: More material is needed to halve the intensity of a high-energy beam.

q: HVL is most commonly expressed in:
explain: Aluminium is the reference material for diagnostic X-ray beam quality.

q: Beam quality in diagnostic radiography is primarily determined by:
explain: These two set the spectrum and therefore the penetrating ability.

q: Beam quantity (intensity) is mainly controlled by:
explain: Photon number is proportional to mA × time.

q: According to the inverse square law, if the distance from the source doubles, the intensity becomes:
An exposure of 10 mAs at 100 cm SID. To keep the same receptor exposure at 200 cm SID, the mAs required is:
explain: mAs must be multiplied by (200/100)^2 = 4.

q: The 15% rule states that:
options: Increasing kVp by 15% halves the mAs
Increasing kVp by 15% has about the same effect on exposure as doubling mAs
kVp must never change by more than 15%
explain: A 15% rise in kVp doubles receptor exposure; a 15% fall halves it.

q: To halve the receptor exposure using the 15% rule, you would:
explain: A 15% reduction in kVp halves the exposure.

q: The reciprocity law states that the receptor exposure depends on:
options: The product of mA and time (mAs), not on the individual values
explain: Different mA/time combinations that give the same mAs produce the same exposure (for digital and screen-film at ordinary times).

q: The best way to reduce motion unsharpness is to:
explain: A shorter exposure freezes patient movement; mA is increased to compensate.

q: Compared with a low-kVp technique, a high-kVp technique gives:
options: Higher patient dose and higher contrast
Lower patient dose and lower subject contrast
explain: More penetrating beams give less absorption (lower dose) and less differential attenuation.

q: The primary purpose of beam collimation is to:
options: Increase the contrast of the grid
Reduce patient dose and scatter radiation
explain: A smaller irradiated volume produces less scatter and a lower integral dose.

q: Positive beam limitation (PBL) automatically:
options: Adjusts the collimator to the size of the image receptor
explain: Sensors in the cassette holder detect cassette size, and the shutters follow it.

q: Which of the following is NOT a beam-restricting device?
explain: Compensating filters change beam intensity across the field and do not restrict its size.

q: The light beam of a collimator must coincide with the X-ray field within:
explain: This is a standard QA tolerance for collimator alignment.

q: The usual SID for a PA chest radiograph is:
explain: The longer SID reduces heart magnification and geometric blur.

q: The standard SID for most general radiographic examinations is:
explain: Most routine projections use about 100 cm (40 inches); chest uses 180 cm (72 inches).

q: The minimum source-to-skin distance generally required for mobile X-ray units is:
explain: A minimum distance prevents high skin entrance doses; fixed fluoroscopy units need at least 38 cm (15 in).

q: Why is the object placed as close to the image receptor as possible?
options: To reduce magnification and geometric unsharpness
explain: A short OID reduces penumbra and magnification.

q: Wedge (compensating) filters are used to:
options: Even out receptor exposure across parts of differing thickness
explain: They attenuate the beam more over thin parts.

q: Which element is mostly used for added filtration in general radiography?
explain: Aluminium removes low-energy photons effectively without too much beam attenuation.

q: Copper filters are sometimes added to aluminium in fluoroscopy and paediatric work to:
options: Remove more low-energy photons and reduce skin dose
explain: Copper is more efficient at hardening the beam.

q: Entrance skin dose is lowered most efficiently by:
options: Using lower kVp and higher mAs
explain: Low-energy photons add skin dose but do not reach the receptor.

q: Automatic exposure control (AEC) terminates the exposure when:
options: A preset dose reaches the detector
explain: Ionisation chambers (or solid-state sensors) measure the radiation and end the exposure.

q: Where are AEC ionisation chambers positioned?
options: Between the patient and the image receptor
explain: They are radiolucent and sit in front of the receptor.

q: The 'backup time' on an AEC system is designed to:
options: Terminate the exposure if the AEC fails
explain: It protects the patient from overexposure if the chamber is incorrectly positioned.

q: Which statement is correct for AEC use?
options: Correct selection of the chamber and positioning of the patient over it is essential
AEC removes the need for collimation
explain: The chamber must be covered by the area of interest.

q: In a fixed kVp (variable mAs) technique chart:
options: mAs is fixed and kVp varies
kVp is set for the body part and mAs is changed with patient thickness
explain: It gives consistent contrast across patient sizes.

q: Which exposure factor mainly affects the penetration of the beam through the patient?
explain: Higher kVp increases photon energy.

q: Increasing mAs will primarily change:
explain: More photons reduce quantum noise; contrast is largely unchanged.

q: Doubling the mAs approximately doubles the:
explain: Dose is proportional to the number of photons.

q: The intensity of scatter radiation produced increases with:
options: Increasing kVp, field size and patient thickness
explain: More tissue irradiated and more high-energy photons produce more Compton scatter.

q: Backscatter from the patient's skin surface contributes to:
explain: The skin exposure is about 1.3-1.4 times higher than the incident air kerma because of backscatter.

q: The inverse square law applies to:
options: A point source with no attenuation
explain: It holds in air for a small source.

q: A radiograph is taken at 90 cm SID with 12 mAs. For the same receptor exposure at 120 cm SID the new mAs is approximately:
The 'mAs' of an exposure of 200 mA for 0.05 s is:
Which exposure time is needed for 25 mAs at 500 mA?
explain: time = mAs / mA = 25/500 = 0.05 s.

q: The kVp is increased from 60 to 69 kVp. The mAs should be changed by what factor to maintain the same receptor exposure?
explain: 69 is 15% above 60, so exposure doubles and mAs is halved.

q: Rise in kVp has what effect on exposure latitude in film-screen imaging?
options: Increases latitude (wider range of acceptable exposure)
explain: A flatter scale of contrast tolerates more exposure variation.

q: Air kerma is measured in:
explain: Kerma is the kinetic energy released in a mass of air, 1 Gy = 1 J/kg.

q: Dose-area product (DAP) is expressed in:
explain: DAP is the air kerma multiplied by the beam area, and it is independent of distance.

q: The advantage of DAP meters is that they:
options: Are independent of the distance from the source
explain: Dose falls by the inverse square and the area rises by the same factor.

q: Diagnostic reference levels (DRLs) are used to:
options: Set legal dose limits for patients
Identify unusually high patient doses for a typical examination
explain: They are investigation levels for optimisation, not dose limits.

q: Which one is a patient dose-reduction technique?
options: Gonad shielding where appropriate and tight collimation
explain: Collimation and shielding reduce unnecessary irradiation.

q: Compared to PA, an AP projection of the chest gives the heart:
explain: The heart is farther from the receptor in AP projections.

q: Why is a PA chest preferred to an AP chest?
options: Less heart magnification and less dose to the breast and thyroid region
explain: The heart is closer to the receptor, and the PA direction lowers dose to anterior organs such as the breast and thyroid.

q: The angle of the central ray for the tube angulation is measured relative to:
explain: Angulation is described with respect to the perpendicular to the receptor.

q: The typical exposure time for chest radiography is very short mainly to:
options: Reduce motion of the heart and lungs
explain: Short exposures freeze cardiac and respiratory movement.

q: A high-kVp chest technique (110-125 kVp) is used to:
options: Demonstrate lung markings with reduced rib contrast
explain: High kVp reduces bone-soft tissue contrast so the lungs are better seen.

q: Mobile radiography units typically use which type of generator?
options: None, they use only gamma rays
explain: They need to operate without a high-capacity mains supply.

q: A capacitor-discharge mobile unit has a falling kVp during the exposure because:
options: The capacitor voltage drops as it discharges
explain: The charge is depleted as the exposure goes on.

q: The relationship between photon energy (keV) and wavelength (nm) is:
explain: Wavelength in nm equals 1.24 divided by the energy in keV.

q: The unit used for the output of a diagnostic X-ray tube per mAs is typically:
explain: Tube output is measured as air kerma per mAs at a set distance.

q: Subject contrast is determined mainly by:
options: Differences in attenuation within the patient and beam energy (kVp)
explain: It depends on the object (thickness, density, atomic number) and the beam quality.

q: Photoelectric absorption in tissue is proportional to approximately:
explain: It rises rapidly with atomic number and falls rapidly with energy, which gives good contrast at low kVp.

q: The dominant interaction in soft tissue at diagnostic energies of about 60-100 keV is:
explain: Compton scattering predominates in soft tissue above about 30 keV.

q: The Compton effect depends mainly on:
explain: It is largely independent of Z, and depends on the number of electrons per gram.

q: Which statement about lowering kVp is correct?
options: Contrast rises and patient dose rises
explain: More photoelectric absorption raises contrast but also absorbed dose.

q: K-edge of iodine is approximately:
explain: Iodine contrast attenuates strongly just above 33 keV.

q: K-edge of barium is approximately:
explain: Barium has a K-edge of about 37.4 keV.

q: The spatial resolution of a system is commonly expressed as:
explain: A higher number of line pairs means finer detail.

q: The modulation transfer function (MTF) describes:
options: How well a system reproduces contrast at different spatial frequencies
explain: An MTF of 1 means perfect transfer; it falls with increasing spatial frequency.

q: The limiting spatial resolution is usually quoted at an MTF of about:
explain: Beyond 10% the contrast is usually too low to be perceived.

q: Geometric unsharpness (penumbra) is calculated as:
explain: Penumbra widens with a large focal spot and a large object-image distance.

q: Magnification factor (MF) equals:
explain: Magnification is the image size over the object size, which equals SID/SOD.

q: An object lies 80 cm from the focal spot and the SID is 100 cm. The magnification factor is:
To reduce geometric unsharpness one should:
options: Use a smaller focal spot and increase SID
explain: These reduce the width of the penumbra.

q: Which of the following improves spatial resolution?
explain: Smaller pixels sample finer detail.

q: The Nyquist frequency of a digital detector with a pixel pitch of 0.1 mm is:
explain: fN = 1 / (2 × pitch) = 1 / 0.2 mm = 5 lp/mm.

q: A digital detector with a 0.2 mm pixel pitch has a Nyquist frequency of:
Quantum mottle is caused by:
options: Too few X-ray photons forming the image
explain: Statistical fluctuation in photon number appears as noise.

q: Increasing the number of photons detected by a factor of 4 changes the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) by a factor of:
explain: SNR is proportional to the square root of the number of photons.

q: The contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) is:
options: The difference in signal between two regions divided by the noise
explain: It determines detectability of low-contrast lesions.

q: Detective quantum efficiency (DQE) expresses:
options: How efficiently a detector converts input photon information to output signal
explain: A higher DQE gives better image quality at the same dose.

q: The major sources of noise in a radiograph include:
explain: Quantum mottle dominates at low exposure; electronic noise matters in digital detectors.

q: Which change will reduce image noise?
explain: More photons reach the detector.

q: The use of a grid is mainly to:
options: Reduce scattered radiation reaching the receptor and improve contrast
explain: Absorbing scatter improves contrast, at the cost of a higher dose.

q: Typical grid ratios in general radiography are:
explain: Higher ratios clean up scatter better but need more exposure.

q: The grid frequency is:
options: The speed of the grid movement
The number of lead strips per centimetre
explain: Usual values are about 40-80 lines/cm.

q: The Bucky factor (grid conversion factor) is:
options: The ratio of kVp with and without a grid
The ratio of SID to SOD
The ratio of exposure with a grid to the exposure without a grid for the same receptor dose
explain: It reflects the increase in patient dose; typical values are 3-5.

q: If an exposure of 10 mAs is used without a grid and the Bucky factor is 5, the mAs with the grid is:
Which statement is TRUE of a higher-ratio grid?
options: It has better scatter removal but more positioning sensitivity
explain: Alignment tolerances get tighter with increasing grid ratio.

q: Grid cut-off is caused by:
options: Misalignment of the grid, wrong SID or off-centring
explain: Primary photons are absorbed by the lead strips.

q: A focused grid must be used at the:
explain: The lead strips are angled to align with the diverging beam at a given distance.

q: Using a focused grid at the wrong SID (off-focus error) produces:
options: Progressive loss of exposure toward the edges of the image
Loss of exposure at the centre only
explain: The angled lead strips no longer line up with the diverging beam, so peripheral primary photons are absorbed.

q: The interspace material in modern grids is usually:
explain: These absorb less primary radiation than older materials like paper or wood.

q: The lead strips in a grid are made of:
explain: Lead strongly absorbs the oblique scattered photons.

q: A moving grid (Potter-Bucky) is used to:
explain: Movement during the exposure blurs the strips so they are not visible.

q: A grid is generally recommended when the part thickness exceeds about:
explain: Thicker parts and above 60 kVp produce considerable scatter.

q: The air-gap technique reduces scatter by:
options: Increasing the object-to-receptor distance so scatter misses the receptor
explain: It is the alternative to the grid but causes magnification.

q: Which will increase the scatter radiation reaching the receptor?
explain: More tissue volume is irradiated.

q: Scatter fraction is the:
options: Proportion of heat in the anode
Proportion of scattered photons in the total radiation reaching the receptor
explain: A high scatter fraction lowers image contrast.

q: Image distortion due to unequal magnification results from:
options: Object parts at different distances from the receptor or tilting
explain: Parts further from the receptor are magnified more.

q: Elongation distortion occurs when:
options: The tube and receptor are parallel to the part
The tube or the receptor is angled to the part
explain: The image is longer than the object.

q: Foreshortening is caused by:
options: Angulation of the object (the part is not parallel to the receptor)
explain: The part appears shorter than its true length.

q: The primary factor affecting motion unsharpness is:
explain: Both voluntary and involuntary motion cause blur.

q: Which of these gives the sharpest image?
options: Small focal spot, long SID, short OID
Large focal spot, short SID, long OID
Large focal spot, long SID, short OID
Small focal spot, short SID, long OID
explain: These choices all minimise geometric unsharpness.

q: The 'Anode-side' of the field has better sharpness because the:
options: Effective focal spot is smaller on the anode side
explain: The effective focal spot size varies along the anode-cathode axis; it is smaller toward the anode.

q: Beam hardening is:
options: A fall in the average energy
A rise in the number of photons
A rise in the average energy of the beam as it passes through material
explain: Low-energy photons are preferentially absorbed.

q: Which type of contrast may be changed after the exposure in digital radiography?
explain: Digital post-processing adjusts the displayed greyscale.

q: Rise in patient thickness leads to:
explain: More tissue absorbs more primary photons and produces more scatter.

q: The phosphor most widely used in modern rare-earth intensifying screens is:
explain: Rare-earth screens convert X-rays to light with greater efficiency than calcium tungstate.

q: Gd2O2S:Tb screens emit light mainly in the:
explain: They require green-sensitive film (orthochromatic).

q: Calcium tungstate screens emit light mainly in the:
explain: They need blue-sensitive film.

q: Compared to direct X-ray exposure, intensifying screens:
options: Reduce the radiation required to expose the film
explain: Light from screens produces more than 95% of the film blackening.

q: Increasing screen speed generally:
options: Reduces patient dose but reduces spatial resolution
explain: Thicker phosphor layers are more efficient but spread light more.

q: A speed-400 screen-film system compared with speed 200 needs:
explain: Relative speed is inversely proportional to the exposure required.

q: The characteristic (H&D) curve of film shows the relationship between:
explain: It is a plot of density against the log of relative exposure.

q: The slope of the straight-line portion of the characteristic curve is the film's:
explain: A steep curve means high contrast and low latitude.

q: Optical density of 2.0 transmits what fraction of the light?
explain: OD = log10 (I0/It), so OD 2 means 1/100 is transmitted.

q: The order of the steps in manual film processing is:
explain: The latent image is developed first and then fixed.

q: The role of the fixer is to:
options: Remove unexposed silver halide and harden the emulsion
explain: The fixer clears the film and makes the image permanent.

q: The developing agents in film developer are:
explain: These reduce exposed silver halide crystals to metallic silver.

q: Film fog is:
options: Unwanted density not caused by the image exposure
explain: Causes include age, heat, scatter and safelight leakage.

q: Film latitude is:
options: The range of exposures that give acceptable densities
explain: Low-contrast films have wide latitude.

q: The photostimulable phosphor used in computed radiography (CR) is:
explain: BaFBr:Eu stores the energy of absorbed X-rays as a latent image.

q: In CR, the latent image on the imaging plate is read out by:
explain: The stimulated phosphor emits blue light that is collected and digitised.

q: Light emitted from a CR plate during readout is:
explain: A red laser (about 633 nm) stimulates emission of blue light (about 400 nm).

q: After readout a CR imaging plate is:
options: Erased with bright light so it can be reused
explain: Intense white light removes residual energy.

q: Which describes direct-conversion digital radiography (DR)?
options: X-rays are first converted to light by caesium iodide
Image is read out by a laser
X-rays are converted directly into electric charge by amorphous selenium
explain: No intermediate light step means less lateral spreading.

q: Indirect-conversion flat-panel detectors typically use:
options: A caesium iodide scintillator with an amorphous silicon photodiode array
explain: The scintillator converts X-rays to light, and photodiodes convert the light to charge.

q: The thin-film transistor (TFT) in a flat-panel detector is used to:
options: Read out the charge from each detector element
explain: A TFT switch on each pixel allows readout.

q: Fill factor of a flat-panel detector is the:
options: Fraction of the pixel area that is sensitive to radiation
explain: A higher fill factor increases efficiency and dose utilisation.

q: The bit depth of a digital image determines the:
options: Number of grey levels that can be displayed
explain: A 12-bit image has 2^12 = 4096 grey levels.

q: The number of grey levels in a 14-bit image is:
Image matrix size of 2048 × 2048 contains how many pixels in total?
Windowing in digital imaging adjusts the:
options: Contrast and brightness of the displayed image
explain: Window width controls contrast and window level controls brightness.

q: In digital radiography, a wide dynamic range means that the detector:
options: Responds linearly across a large range of exposures
explain: It reduces retakes caused by incorrect exposure.

q: Under-exposure in digital imaging typically results in:
explain: Fewer photons increase quantum mottle; the image brightness is adjusted automatically.

q: Over-exposure in digital radiography:
options: Always makes the image very dark
May go unnoticed because of automatic rescaling, but increases the patient dose
explain: This is known as 'dose creep'.

q: Exposure index (EI) in digital radiography indicates:
options: The detector exposure level for the image
explain: It helps technologists to detect under- or over-exposure.

q: Image archiving and communication in hospitals is handled by:
explain: Picture Archiving and Communication System.

q: The standard format for exchanging medical images is:
explain: Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine.

q: Unlike film, a digital image processed with an edge-enhancement algorithm shows:
options: Improved visibility of edges but possibly increased noise
explain: Edge enhancement emphasises high spatial frequencies, including noise.

q: In an image intensifier, the input phosphor is made of:
explain: Needle-like CsI crystals give high absorption and little light spread.

q: The output phosphor of an image intensifier is:
explain: ZnCdS:Ag produces light for the video camera or optics.

q: The photocathode in an image intensifier:
explain: It is made of antimony-caesium compounds.

q: Electrons in an image intensifier are accelerated through approximately:
explain: This raises the electron energy and so the brightness.

q: Brightness gain of an image intensifier equals:
explain: Minification gain is the ratio of the input and output screen areas.

q: If the input diameter is 25 cm and the output diameter is 2.5 cm, the minification gain is:
explain: The ratio of areas = (25/2.5)² = 100.

q: Switching an image intensifier to a smaller field-of-view (magnification) mode will:
options: Increase the patient dose and improve the resolution
Reduce the dose and improve the resolution
explain: Less minification means that more radiation is needed to maintain brightness.

q: Automatic brightness control (ABC) in fluoroscopy adjusts:
options: kVp and/or mA to maintain image brightness
explain: It is a feedback system based on the output brightness.

q: Pincushion distortion is associated with:
explain: The curved input screen causes distortion at the periphery; flat panels avoid this.

q: Which fluoroscopic detector avoids vignetting and geometric distortion?
explain: Flat panels have a uniform response across the field.

q: Pulsed fluoroscopy reduces patient dose by:
options: Decreasing the number of exposures per second
Increasing the kVp to its maximum
explain: Fewer pulses mean less radiation in a given time.

q: The last-image-hold function in fluoroscopy:
options: Reduces dose by displaying the last frame without exposure
explain: It lets the operator review the image with no further radiation.

q: In digital subtraction angiography (DSA), the mask image is:
options: An image with a lead mask
An image acquired before the contrast agent is injected
An image of the contrast only
explain: Subtracting it from contrast images isolates the vessels.

q: The cumulative timer in fluoroscopy sounds an alarm after:
explain: It reminds the operator of the cumulative fluoroscopy time.

q: The usual maximum entrance exposure rate for normal-mode fluoroscopy is:
explain: High-level-control modes may allow up to 20 R/min (about 176 mGy/min).

q: The minimum source-to-skin distance for fixed fluoroscopic units is:
explain: It prevents high skin doses.

q: In a fluoroscopy suite, the under-couch tube configuration usually gives the operator:
options: Higher scatter exposure to the eyes
Lower scatter exposure to the head and chest
explain: Scatter is highest near the entrance surface, which is below the table.

q: The best way for staff to reduce their dose during fluoroscopy is to:
options: Stand right at the table side without a lead apron
Increase distance from the patient and use shielding
explain: Time, distance and shielding are the three basic principles.

q: A wire mesh test is used to check:
explain: Areas of poor contact appear as blurred regions on the image of the mesh.

q: A star test pattern, pinhole or slit camera is used to measure the:
explain: These quality control tests determine the focal spot size and its blooming.

q: The accuracy of the kVp of an X-ray unit is usually acceptable within:
explain: Tolerances vary by guideline, but typically are within 5-10%.

q: Reproducibility (consistency) of X-ray output under repeated identical exposures is acceptable if the coefficient of variation is less than:
explain: Output should be consistent from one exposure to another.

q: A reject (repeat) analysis programme is used to:
options: Identify the causes of repeated radiographs and reduce unnecessary dose
explain: It is a quality assurance tool that includes positioning errors and exposure errors.

q: Lead aprons for staff in diagnostic radiology should have a minimum of:
explain: 0.25 mm is the minimum, 0.35-0.5 mm is common.
